[1] Anyone who walks past one of our city's elementary schools at recess in late May will notice the same scene: dozens of children packed into the thin strip of shadow along the building's north wall. The rest of the playground, a broad sheet of asphalt and rubber matting, sits nearly empty. The children have not lost interest in the swings. By late morning, the metal slide is simply too hot to touch.

[2] We believe the city should plant shade trees on every school playground, and we believe it should begin this fall. The case is not complicated, asphalt in direct summer sun can become far hotter than the air above it, hot enough to ignite a child's palm. The shade under a row of maples keep the ground beneath it many degrees cooler. Children notice that difference long before any thermometer records it.

[3] Trees would also save money. Shaded windows keep classrooms cooler, which lowers the districts cooling bills in the warmest months. Nadia Ferrante, who manages building maintenance for the district, estimates that rubber matting kept out of direct sun lasts several years longer than matting left exposed. Because shaded matting cracks less, the district would replace fewer sections each year.

[4] Therefore, a young tree asks something of us. A sapling needs regular watering through its first few summers, and someone has to keep to that schedule after school lets out in June. Critics are right that a new tree is a total pain to look after. But parent groups at three of our schools have already offered to organize summer watering crews, and the city's forestry office plants and tends hundreds of street trees every year. The work is real, but it is not new.

[5] Shade is not a decoration on a playground; it is what makes a playground usable in the very months when children most want to be outside. We are asking the city council to fund the first two hundred trees in next year's budget.
prompt: In paragraph 3, in the sentence "Because shaded matting cracks less, the district would replace fewer sections each year," which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable in place of "fewer sections"?
explanation: "Sections" is a countable plural noun, so "fewer" is the correct comparative, as written. "Less" is used for amounts that are not counted one by one (as in "cracks less" earlier in the sentence), so "less sections" is a usage error. "Lesser" means smaller in importance or quality, not smaller in number, so "lesser sections" changes the meaning to lower-grade sections. "The fewest" is a superlative, which requires a comparison among three or more things that the sentence never sets up.

passage:
[1] On early summer nights in parts of the Great Smoky Mountains, a stretch of forest can go dark and bright as if someone were working a light switch. Thousands of fireflies of one species, Photinus carolinus, flash together in short bursts, pause in darkness for several seconds, and then flash together again. Visitors who have seen the display often describes it as a wave of light rolling through the trees.

[2] Synchrony like this is unusual. Most fireflies flash on their own schedules, a male signaling and a female answering from the grass. Only a small number of species, found mainly in Southeast Asia and North America, gather together in groups that flash in unison, all at the same moment. In some Southeast Asian species, males crowd into a single tree along a riverbank, and flash so closely together that the whole tree seems to blink.

[3] How do the insects stay together? No single firefly leads the others. The explanation researchers favor is that each male has an internal rhythm that sets the pace of his flashes. [A] That rhythm, however, is not fixed. [B] Each adjustment is tiny, but a male makes one every time a neighbor lights up. [C] Over a few minutes, thousands of these small corrections pull an entire hillside onto a single beat. [D]

[4] Why synchronize at all? One explanation that researchers have tested involves the females, which stay low and answer the males from below. A lone male's flash is easy to lose in a forest at night. Nevertheless, a female watching from the ground may miss it entirely. When many males flash at once and then go dark together. The pattern stands out against the background.

[5] The display has two parts: a burst of quick flashes and a dark pause that follows. Females answer only when they recognize the timing of their own species, and a shared pause makes that timing easier to read. In one set of experiments, researchers showed females small lights programmed to blink in different patterns and find that the females answered the synchronized patterns far more often than the scattered ones.
prompt: The writer wants to add the following sentence to paragraph 3: "When a male sees a neighbor flash, he moves his own next flash slightly earlier or later to bring the two closer together." For the sake of logic and cohesion, the sentence should be placed at:
explanation: The sentence explains how a male's rhythm changes, so it belongs right after "That rhythm, however, is not fixed," which raises the question, and right before "Each adjustment is tiny," whose phrase "Each adjustment" needs the shift just described as its referent. Point [B] is the only place that satisfies both. At Point [A] the adjustment would be described before the paragraph says the rhythm is not fixed, which makes the "however" that follows illogical. At Point [C] "Each adjustment" would appear with nothing yet adjusted. At Point [D] the sentence would follow the paragraph's conclusion about a whole hillside keeping a single beat, explaining a mechanism after its result.

passage:
[1] In the summer of 1858, the river through London began to smell so strongly that people crossing its bridges held cloths over their faces. The city's household drains and overflowing cesspits had emptied into the Thames, and during that unusually hot June the low water left the waste baking in the sun. Newspapers soon gave the episode a name. They called it the Great Stink.

[2] The smell reached even the Houses of Parliament, which stood on the riverbank at Westminster. Members tried soaking the building's curtains in chemicals to block the odor, and some talked of moving their sessions out of London altogether. Westminster Abbey, which stands nearby, had been the site of English coronations since the eleventh century. In contrast, lawmakers who had put off the problem for years passed a bill giving the Metropolitan Board of Works the money and authority to build new sewers.

[3] The engineer chosen for the job was Joseph Bazalgette, whose plans had been stalled for two years by arguments over cost. His solution was to intercept the waste. He designed large sewers that ran parallel to the river they caught the old drains before those drains could reach the Thames. The sewers then carried the flow east to outfalls, which were located many miles downstream at a considerable distance from the city. He also made the pipes far larger than the city then needed—a choice that let the system keep up with a population that grew well beyond what anyone in 1858 had predicted.

[4] The work required digging tunnels, laying hundreds of millions of bricks, and the construction of pumping stations to lift the waste where the ground was too flat for gravity. Along the north bank, the Victoria Embankment was built partly to hold one of the main sewers. Once the main lines were finished in the 1870s the river through central London no longer received most of the city's sewage. Much of that network still carries London's waste today.

[5] Bazalgette did not know that cholera spreads through contaminated water; like most engineers of his day, he blamed foul air. Yet by carrying sewage away from the crowded center, his system helped end the cholera outbreaks that had struck London several times in earlier decades.
prompt: In paragraph 2, in the sentence "In contrast, lawmakers who had put off the problem for years passed a bill giving the Metropolitan Board of Works the money and authority to build new sewers," which choice provides the most logical transition in place of "In contrast,"?
explanation: The paragraph tells a sequence: the smell reached Parliament, members tried to block it, and then lawmakers acted. "Within a few weeks" places the bill in that order and stresses how quickly the long delay ended. "In contrast" sets the bill against the members' efforts as if the two were opposites, when the bill followed from them. "For example" would make passing the bill an instance of soaking curtains or talking of leaving. "Similarly" calls the bill another attempt of the same kind, when it was the decisive step.

passage_title: The Forge in the Truck Bed
passage:
[1] Rosalind Petrakis starts most mornings in a pickup truck that carries a propane forge, an anvil, and a load of steel. She is a farrier, and on a typical day she trims and shoes horses at four or five barns. Most of her clients are boarding stables near the county line, a few are families who keep a single pony behind the house.

[2] Petrakis learned the trade during a three-year apprenticeship in Kentucky. Like a fingernail, the outer wall of a hoof grows continuously, about a quarter of an inch a month. A horse running free on rough ground erases that growth on its own, but a horse ridden across soft pasture does not. Every six to eight weeks, Petrakis pulls each shoe, trims the excess wall, and resets or replaces the shoe. The owners of each horse, who usually hold the lead rope while she works, have learned to book her next visit before she leaves.

[3] Shoeing begins with the trim. [A] Petrakis lifts each foot between her knees, scrapes out the dirt, and pares the wall back with nippers. [B] She heats a shoe until it glows orange and hammers it on the anvil to match the hoof's outline. [C] Before driving any nails, she presses the hot shoe against the hoof, and the scorched ring it leaves shows her where the fit is off. [D] The nails angle through the outer wall, which has no nerves, and she bends their tips over and files them smooth.

[4] Petrakis says the hardest part of the job has little to do with steel. She has shod hundreds of horses, and she keeps a notebook of each animals' habits: which one leans, which one bites, which one hates the hiss of the forge. Calm handlers make calm horses, she says. For instance, a mare that once fought her every visit now dozes on three legs, because her owner stopped pacing the aisle. When a horse is nervous, Petrakis asks the owner to stand between the horse and she.

[5] At fifty-one, Petrakis knows her body will not keep this pace forever. Her shoulders ache most evenings. She has started training an apprentice. Watching from the doorway, a spiral notebook fills up with the apprentice's sketches of every hoof, the way Petrakis once filled her own.
prompt: In paragraph 5, in the sentence "Watching from the doorway, a spiral notebook fills up with the apprentice's sketches of every hoof, the way Petrakis once filled her own," which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable in place of "a spiral notebook fills up with the apprentice's sketches of every hoof"?
choices: the apprentice fills a spiral notebook with sketches of every hoof
sketches of every hoof fill up the apprentice's spiral notebook
the apprentice's spiral notebook fills up with sketches of every hoof
correct_answer: the apprentice fills a spiral notebook with sketches of every hoof
explanation: An introductory participial phrase modifies the subject that follows it, and the one "watching from the doorway" is the apprentice, so the apprentice must be the subject: "the apprentice fills a spiral notebook with sketches of every hoof." This also matches the closing comparison, since Petrakis "once filled her own." As written, the notebook is the one watching. Making "sketches" the subject has the sketches watching. "The apprentice's spiral notebook" still makes the notebook the subject; the possessive "apprentice's" only modifies "notebook" and cannot serve as the subject the phrase describes.

passage:
[1] For most of my thirties I hiked the way I drove; by following a blue dot on a screen. The dot never once got me lost, which is why it took me so long to notice how little I knew about where I actually was.

[2] The change began on a three-day trip in the high desert, when my phone's battery dies on the first afternoon. My friend Tobias, who had been hiking that country since college, pulled a folded paper map and a scuffed compass out of his pack. I expected him to take over. Therefore, he handed both to me and said he would follow wherever I led.

[3] The first lessons were humbling. A compass needle points to magnetic north, which in that part of the West sits several degrees away from the true north printed on the map. Tobias showed me how to correct for the difference and lining up the edge of the compass with a ridge I could see. I made mistakes a child would have caught. Twice I sighted on the wrong peak, and once I walked confident and quickly for a mile in exactly the wrong direction.

[4] Reading the map, it turned out, meant reading the land first. Contour lines, the thin brown curves that connect points of equal elevation, crowds together where a slope is steep and spread apart where it is gentle. On the second day I spotted a dark smudge of them on the route I had chosen, and we swung half a mile east rather than walk to the edge of a forty-foot drop.

[5] By the last morning I was choosing our route myself, and Tobias was trailing behind with his hands in his pockets. I still carry my phone on every hike, charged and switched off at the bottom of my pack. However, I no longer reach for it first. What the map gave me was not a better way of getting somewhere but a picture of the place I was moving through, and I would not trade that picture for any blue dot.
prompt: In paragraph 1, in the sentence "For most of my thirties I hiked the way I drove; by following a blue dot on a screen," which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable in place of "drove; by following"?
explanation: What follows "the way I drove" explains what that way was, and a colon after a complete independent clause correctly introduces such an explanation, even when the explanation is only a phrase. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and "by following a blue dot on a screen" is not one. A period leaves "By following a blue dot on a screen" standing alone as a sentence fragment. Inserting "it was" after a comma turns the phrase into an independent clause joined to the first with only a comma, which is a comma splice.

passage:
[1] A river that falls a few hundred feet over its course poses no problem for the water, but it poses a serious one for a boat. Rapids, falls, and shallows interrupt the route, and a canal cut beside the river must somehow climb or descend the same height. The usual answer is the lock, a device so simple that its basic design has changed little in centuries.

[2] Locks can be found on canals in dozens of countries, from England to China. A lock is a long, watertight chamber with a pair of gates at each end. The gates of each pair meet at an angle that points upstream, so the weight of the water on the higher side presses them shut rather than forcing them open. Set into the gates are paddles—small sliding panels—that let water into or out of the chamber.

[3] [A] To raise a boat, the keeper first lets the chamber drain to the level of the lower canal and opens their lower gates. [B] The boat motors in, and the gates swing closed behind it. [C] Then the paddles in the upper gates were opened, and water from the higher canal pours into the chamber, lifting the boat. [D] When the water inside matches the level outside, the upper gates open and the boat continues on its way.

[4] Lowering a boat simply reverses the order. The boat enters a full chamber from above, the upper gates close behind it, and the keeper raises the lower paddles. The water drains out downward into the lower canal until the two levels match, and the lower gates swing open. Each time a boat passes, then, a full chamber of water flows from the upper canal toward the lower one. Instead, the highest stretch of a canal loses water to leaks and evaporation, so engineers feed it from streams or reservoirs to keep it full.

[5] Because each step uses gravity rather than an engine a lock can keep working for a century with little more than new gates every few decades. Some flights of locks in Britain, built more than two hundred years ago, still lift boats today. Each chamber in such a flight holding back a little more of the hillside. Climbing one takes hours, but no part of the climb needs a pump.
prompt: In paragraph 5, in the sentence "Because each step uses gravity rather than an engine a lock can keep working for a century with little more than new gates every few decades," which choice is correctly punctuated in place of "engine a lock"?
explanation: "Because each step uses gravity rather than an engine" is an introductory dependent clause, and a comma should separate it from the main clause, "a lock can keep working." Without the comma, "an engine a lock" runs together. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and the "Because" clause is not one. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, which the "Because" clause is not.

passage:
[1] On screen, a felt fox trots across a kitchen table in one easy stride that lasts about two seconds. Behind the camera, the fox is a puppet about the size of a teacup. Stop-motion animation is built from still photographs, and each photograph records a puppet that someone has nudged by hand, often by less than a millimeter. Played back quickly, the photographs blend into movement.

[2] Film is projected at twenty-four frames per second, most animators save labor by shooting on twos, holding each pose for two frames so that a second of movement needs only twelve poses. Even at that rate, the arithmetic is unforgiving. A ten-second shot requires more than a hundred adjustments, each photographed before the next can begin. Animators, which often spend days alone on a single shot, learn to think in frames rather than seconds.

[3] The puppets are built for this patience. Under the felt or silicone skin of most professional puppets is an armature. An armature is a metal skeleton whose ball-and-socket joints are stiff enough to hold any position. Small bolts called tie-downs fasten a puppets feet to the sets floor, so that the figure cannot topple while the animator reaches across it.

[4] The real difficulty is consistency. If a limb travels farther between two frames than between the previous two, the movement lurches, and viewers notice even when they cannot say why. Frame-grabbing software helps by laying a faint image of the previous frame over the camera's live view, a feature called onion skinning. However, the animator sees the old pose and the new one at the same moment and can compare them. When every increment is right, the finished motion will look smoothly and natural.

[5] All of this makes stop-motion slow even by the standards of animation. On a feature film, a single animator may finish only a few seconds of footage in a full day, and often less. Yet many directors, and a good share of their audiences, are drawn to the form for that very reason. A puppet handled thousands of times keeps faint traces of the hands that moved it: a fingerprint pressed into clay, a ripple in a felt coat. Computer animation can imitate such marks, but in stop-motion they are simply there.
prompt: In paragraph 4, which choice provides the most logical transition in place of "However," in the sentence that begins "However, the animator sees the old pose"?
explanation: The sentence restates what onion skinning does: the faint image of the previous frame laid over the live view means the animator sees the old pose and the new one together. A restatement that clarifies is signaled by "That is." "However" signals a contrast, but this sentence agrees with the one before it. "Instead" signals that one thing replaces another, and nothing is being replaced. "Meanwhile" marks a separate action happening at the same time, but seeing both poses is not a separate event; it is the overlay itself.

passage:
[1] Laundromats are a common sight in most neighborhoods. By this hour you have the Bright Wash on Calder Street nearly to yourself. The fluorescent tubes overhead hum at a pitch you stop hearing after a minute. The attendant—a woman named Marisol who has worked the night shift here for eleven years, keeps a radio on the counter turned so low that the music seems to come from another building. The only other customer is a man in a paint-spattered jacket, asleep in a plastic chair with his arms folded.

[2] You choose a washer near the window, feed it quarters, and listen to it fill. Then there is nothing to do but wait. Which is the part most people dread, and the part you have come to like. You settle into an orange chair by the window. With no call to return and no dish to wash, the next half hour belongs to no one. From that chair you can read every one of the washers timers, their red numbers counting down from different starting points.

[3] Self-service laundries spread across American cities in the middle of the twentieth century. At this hour the room has a rhythm of its own. The row of big dryers along the back wall, only two of them in use, gives off a low and steady thump. Every few minutes a machine finishes its cycle and goes quiet, and the silence it leaves seems louder than the noise did. Before long, your own washer shuddered and stops.

[4] You move the wet load into a dryer, return to the same chair you had sat in before, the one you sat in earlier, and wait again. It is still warm. At last, the dryer buzzes. The towels, that you pull from the drum are hot enough to sting your wrists, and you fold them on the long table under the window. Behind you, the man in the paint-spattered jacket wakes and leaves without a word.

[5] When you finally step outside with your bag, the street is darker than you remember. The clothes against your back are warm and smell of nothing at all. Through the glass you see Marisol turn the radio up a notch, now that the room is hers again.
prompt: In paragraph 3, in the sentence "Before long, your own washer shuddered and stops," which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable in place of "shuddered and stops"?
explanation: The essay narrates in the present tense ("you choose," "you settle," "a machine finishes"), and the two verbs here share one subject, so both must be present and singular: "shudders and stops." The original shifts tense between the two halves of one compound verb. "Shuddered and stopped" is consistent within the sentence but breaks from the present tense of the whole essay. "Shudder and stop" is present tense but plural, so it does not agree with the singular subject "washer."

passage:
[1] In the third century BCE, a scholar in Alexandria measured the size of the whole Earth without ever leaving Egypt. Eratosthenes, who directed the city's famous library, had no ship to carry him around the planet and no way to see its curve. He had three things to work with—a shadow, a report from another city, and some geometry.

[2] The report came from Syene, a town far to the south. Syene lay near the first cataract of the Nile. It was close to the line we now call the Tropic of Cancer. At noon on the summer solstice, people there could look down a deep well and see sunlight on the water at the bottom, which meant that the sun stood directly overhead.

[3] Back in Alexandria, Eratosthenes measured the shadow cast at noon on the same day by a gnomon, an upright pointer like the one on a sundial. [A] The shadow showed that the sun there stood a little over seven degrees from straight overhead. [B] Because the sun is so far away its rays reach the Earth in nearly parallel lines. [C] Those seven degrees, in other words, were also the angle between the two cities as measured from the center of the planet. [D]

[4] Seven degrees is about one-fiftieth of a full circle Eratosthenes concluded that the distance from Syene to Alexandria must be about one-fiftieth of the Earth's circumference. To turn that fraction into a figure, he assumed that Syene lay due south of Alexandria and the distance between the cities being about 5,000 stadia. Multiplying by fifty gave roughly 250,000 stadia, and the arithmetic was simple enough for the library's other scholars and he to check.

[5] Not every assumption held. Syene is not exactly due south of Alexandria, and no one knows precisely how long the stadion he used was. Therefore, his answer came out close to the modern one. Depending on which length historians accept, it was off by somewhere between a few percent and about fifteen percent, a respectable result for a man working with a pointer and a shadow.
prompt: In paragraph 5, in the sentence "Depending on which length historians accept, it was off by somewhere between a few percent and about fifteen percent, a respectable result for a man working with a pointer and a shadow," which choice best maintains the tone of the essay in place of "a respectable result"?
choices: a most estimable and laudable result
explanation: The essay is a plain, measured history; it admires Eratosthenes without exaggeration, and "a respectable result" gives that measured approval as written. "A pretty decent showing" and "a result worth bragging about" are casual, conversational phrases that break the essay's register. "A most estimable and laudable result" swings the other way into inflated, old-fashioned praise, and "estimable" and "laudable" say the same thing twice.

passage_title: A Thousand Voices for a Nation
passage:
[1] A national poll may describe the opinions of an entire country, yet the firm behind it may have spoken to only a thousand people. The method, which statisticians call random sampling has been studied for generations, and it rests on a simple idea: a small group, chosen well, can stand in for a much larger one. The hard part is the choosing.

[2] Choosing well means giving every member of the population the same chance of being picked. Any rule that makes some people easier to reach than others skews the result. Nevertheless, a survey that calls only landline telephones will hear mostly from older households, since many younger adults no longer keep one. The people such a survey misses tends to differ from the ones it reaches in age, in income, and often in their views.

[3] The most famous failure of this kind came in 1936. A popular magazine mailed some ten million mock ballots to Americans whose names it had taken largely from telephone directories and lists of car owners. More than two million came back, and the magazine confidently forecast a victory for Alf Landon. Who lost to Franklin Roosevelt in one of the most lopsided elections in the nation's history. The sample's sheer size had not protected it. During the Depression, households with a telephone or a car were better off than most, and they leaned away from Roosevelt.

[4] Many modern pollsters dial numbers generated at random, so that no list decides who can be reached. Even so, some groups answer more readily than others. When a sample comes back with too few young adults, pollsters adjusted the results, counting each young respondent's answers a little more heavily than the rest. Every survey, then, requires a firm to decide whom to contact, how to reach them, and weighting the answers it gets.

[5] Every reputable poll publishes a margin of error, an estimate of how far its numbers could drift by chance alone. A larger sample narrows that margin, but by less than most people expect. Adding more people does make a poll somewhat more precise. What no amount of size can repair is a sample drawn from the wrong list, as the magazine learned in 1936, when far smaller polls named the winner correctly.
prompt: In paragraph 3, the writer is considering adding the following sentence after the sentence ending "in one of the most lopsided elections in the nation's history": "Landon was the governor of Kansas at the time." Should the writer make this addition here?
choices: Yes, because the paragraph names Landon without saying who he was, and the sentence tells readers what office he held.
Yes, because a sitting governor's record helps explain why the magazine felt confident enough to forecast his victory.
No, because Landon's office has no bearing on why a sample of more than two million ballots produced the wrong forecast.
No, because the sentence would interrupt the paragraph before it reports which candidate actually won the election.
correct_answer: No, because Landon's office has no bearing on why a sample of more than two million ballots produced the wrong forecast.
explanation: Paragraph 3 exists to show why the 1936 poll failed: its lists overrepresented better-off households. Landon's office explains nothing about that failure, so the sentence is a digression and should not be added. It is true that the paragraph names Landon without identifying him, but the essay's point about sampling does not depend on who he was. Nothing in the paragraph ties the magazine's confidence to Landon's record; the confidence came from two million returned ballots. And the sentence would not hold back the outcome, because the sentence it follows has already reported Roosevelt's landslide.

passage:
[1] Old Faithful, the best-known geyser in Yellowstone National Park, does not erupt on a fixed timetable, it keeps a rough schedule instead. Crowds still gather on the benches nearby well before each eruption, because park rangers post a predicted time at the visitor center. The prediction is usually right to within ten minutes or so, which is impressive for an event driven by water boiling deep underground. The reasons the geyser can be forecast at all, and the reasons it cannot be forecast exactly, both lie in its plumbing.

[2] Every geyser needs three things: a source of heat, a supply of water, and a narrow, twisting channel that runs from the surface down toward hot rock. Rain and melted snow seep through cracks in the ground and collect in the channel. The water at the bottom of the channel—pressed down by the weight of all the water above it—can stay liquid at temperatures well above those at which water boils at the surface.

[3] Eventually the water near the bottom grows hot enough to boil anyway. The first bubbles of steam rise and push a little water out of the vent at the top. In contrast, the column above weighs less, and the pressure on the deeper water drops. Suddenly relieved of that weight, the column above flashes into steam, and a roaring jet of water and vapor bursts from the ground. Geysers are found in only a handful of places on Earth.

[4] The length of the wait between eruptions depend mostly on how long the channel takes to refill and reheat. Rangers have learned that a long eruption, tends to be followed by a long wait. They time each eruption and use its duration, meaning how long it lasted, to forecast the next one. Most waits at Old Faithful fall somewhere between about an hour and two hours.

[5] Over longer spans, the schedule itself can shift. Minerals dissolved in the hot water slowly coat the walls of the channel and narrow it, and an earthquake many miles away can rearrange the cracks underground and change a geyser's rhythm for years. A geyser, in the end, is less like a clock than like a kettle that refills itself, and no two refills are quite the same.
prompt: In paragraph 3, in the sentence "Suddenly relieved of that weight, the column above flashes into steam, and a roaring jet of water and vapor bursts from the ground," which choice makes the sentence most logical in place of "the column above"?
explanation: The opening phrase "Suddenly relieved of that weight" must describe the subject that follows it. What loses the weight pressing on it is the deeper water, whose pressure the previous sentence says drops, and it is also the water that can flash into steam. "The column above" is what lost water and grew lighter; it was the weight, not the thing relieved of it. "The first bubbles" are already steam, so they cannot flash into steam, and they rose before the pressure dropped. "The vent" is an opening in the ground, which neither bears that weight nor turns into steam.

passage:
[1] For my sixtieth birthday, my wife, Marguerite, gave me a card with a coupon tucked inside it for eight weeks of ballroom dancing lessons. I had spent thirty-four years as a tax accountant, a profession in which the most strenuous movement is reaching for a calculator. I conveyed my appreciation to her the way a man thanks someone who has just volunteered him for surgery.

[2] The studio occupied the second floor above a hardware store, and its mirrored walls meant that I could watch myself fail from four angles at once. I felt a little uneasy. Our instructor, a silver-haired former competitor named Renzo, went across the floor as if it had been freshly oiled. He paired us off and demonstrated the box step, which he promised anyone could learn in an afternoon.

[3] Marguerite, it turned out, was a natural. She had taken a few lessons as a teenager and seemed to remember every one of them. Similarly, I spent the first hour treating her feet as part of the floor. Renzo watched Marguerite and me for a full minute and then announces that we had what he called potential. He had one piece of advice for me, look at your partner, not at your feet.

[4] By the fourth week I was improving, though more slower than anyone else in the class. I practiced the box step in the kitchen each morning while the coffee brewed, counting under my breath like a man reciting a phone number he is afraid to forget. When the music stopped at the end of the eighth lesson, I realized that I had danced an entire waltz without once looking at my shoes.

[5] Renzo entered us in the studio's spring showcase, where we danced in front of forty strangers and a folding table of lemon bars. I stepped on Marguerite only twice, and she maintains that I meant both of them. We have since signed up for another eight weeks, and I find myself looking forward to Tuesday evenings. I have not mentioned any of this to my former colleagues, who still picture me hunched over a ledger; some things a man prefers to keep off the books.
prompt: In paragraph 3, in the sentence "He had one piece of advice for me, look at your partner, not at your feet," which choice is correctly punctuated in place of "for me, look"?
explanation: "He had one piece of advice for me" is a complete clause, and what follows spells out what the advice was. A dash introduces that explanation: "for me—look at your partner." A comma alone joins the clause to a separate command, which is itself an independent clause, so the original is a comma splice. With no punctuation, the advice runs straight into the clause that announces it. "Which was look" turns the advice into a relative clause, but "was look" is ungrammatical; the clause would need "to look."

[1] A young salmon leaves the stream where it hatched when it is only a few inches long. It travels downstream to the sea, where it may spend several years feeding and growing larger in size. Then, when it is ready to spawn, it does something that has puzzled observers for centuries. Swimming back, against the current, to the very stream where it began.

[2] Scientists now suspect that the journey depends on two different senses, one for the open ocean and one for the final stretch. Far from land, a salmon appears to steer by the Earth's magnetic field. The strength and angle of that field shifts gradually from place to place, so every stretch of coastline carries a slightly different magnetic signature. A fish that registers the signature of its home rivers mouth on the way out can, in principle, steer back toward it years later.

[3] Near the coast, a second sense takes over. [A] While it is still young, a salmon memorizes the scent of its home stream, a chemical blend produced by the soil, plants, and rocks of one watershed. [B] Years later, the returning adult tests the water at every fork in the river, following that address upstream one branch at a time. [C] Biologists call this early learning imprinting. [D]

[4] In the 1950s, a team of biologists, working on a creek in the Pacific Northwest, tested the idea by plugging the noses of salmon caught on their way upstream. Released below a fork in the creek, the biologists found that those fish chose the wrong branch far more often than salmon whose noses had been left open.

[5] Reaching the right stream matters. Most Pacific salmon die within days of spawning, so each fish has a single chance to leave offspring. Even so, a stream's own salmon are suited to it: over many generations, each population has adapted to the temperature, current, and seasonal timing of its home water. A fish that ends up elsewhere may arrive in the wrong season or find gravel unsuited to its eggs.

[6] The system is not flawless. A small share of every run strays into neighboring streams, and these wanderers are probably how salmon colonize new rivers, such as those uncovered by retreating glaciers.

[1] Before 1840, mailing a letter in Britain was costly and confusing. The charges, which rose with every mile a letter traveled and every extra sheet it held, were usually paid by the person who received the letter rather than by the one who sent it. A letter crossing the length of the country could cost more than a shilling, a large share of many workers' daily pay.

[2] Many families found ways to avoid the charge. Because the recipient paid, a sender could mark the outside of a letter with a prearranged sign, such as a dot in one corner or an underlined name. The person at the other end would glance at the sign, learn the news it carried, and hand the letter back unopened, paying nothing. Others sent letters with travelers, this practice broke the law but was rarely punished.

[3] A former schoolteacher named Rowland Hill had helped run his family's school before he turned to other work. Hill laid out his plan in 1837. He did so in a pamphlet called Post Office Reform. In it, he showed that the real cost of a letter lay in receiving it, sorting it, and to deliver it, not in carrying it. Because distance mattered so little, he proposed a single rate of one penny for any letter up to half an ounce, paid in advance by the sender.

[4] The reform changed three things at once; who paid, how the price was figured, and how often ordinary people could afford to write. The Uniform Penny Post began on January 10, 1840, and the Penny Black, the first adhesive postage stamp, went on sale that May. Within a year, the number of letters passing through the mail had roughly doubled.

[5] Letter writing itself began to change. Under the old rates, thrifty writers had often filled a page, turned it sideways, and written a second layer of lines across the first rather than pay for another sheet. However, a letter was now charged by weight, so a writer could usually add a second page at no extra cost. Envelopes, which had once counted as an extra sheet, begin to appear in shops everywhere. Valentines now cost a penny to send, and stationers soon printed it by the thousands.

[1] You arrive at the dock earlier than you need to, wearing a borrowed life jacket and repeating the words you studied the night before: tiller, boom, mainsheet, jib. The boat your instructor points to is about the length of a car, and it rocks when you step near it. The harbor's sailing club, which owns the boat, was founded in the 1920s by a group of local fishermen. Odile, who has taught sailing on this harbor for thirty years, settles into the front of the boat and hands you the tiller.

[2] Her first lesson is that the boat does the opposite of what your hand suggests. Push the tiller to the left, and the bow swings to the right. You know this rule; you read it twice last night. Your arm does not know it, and for ten minutes you zigzag across the harbor like a shopping cart with a bad wheel.

[3] Then a gust arrives. The wind presses on the sail from the side. Similarly, the boat leans until the water is a few inches from the rail. You grip the edge of the seat and laugh at how quickly the shore slides past. Odile only nods, and the look that passes between you and her says that every new sailor grabs that same seat.

[4] Next comes tacking: turning the boat's nose through the wind so the sail fills on the other side. When Odile calls the warning, you push the tiller toward the sail the boat swings its nose across the wind. The most dangerous part of the turn—the second when the sail goes slack, arrives without much warning. The heavy, aluminum boom, swings low across the cockpit, and you duck under it a half second before it would have found your head.

[5] By the sixth tack, the boat feels real steady under you, and Odile has stopped calling out corrections. She tells you that the best sailors she knows capsized most often in their first summer, and that next week you will tip the boat over on purpose. An hour later you sail the boat back to the dock by yourself, on your own, while she sits in the bow and finishes her coffee.
prompt: In paragraph 5, in the sentence "By the sixth tack, the boat feels real steady under you, and Odile has stopped calling out corrections," which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable in place of "real steady"?
explanation: "Feels" here is a linking verb: it connects "the boat" to a word describing the boat, so that word must be the adjective "steady," not the adverb "steadily." The word modifying "steady" says how steady, and a word that modifies an adjective must be an adverb, "really." "Real" is an adjective, so "real steady" and "real steadily" both put it where an adverb is needed; "really steadily" and "real steadily" both put the adverb "steadily" after a linking verb, where an adjective is needed.
